To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
parents are willing to invest heavily in their children's development, particularly those of higher social class, and this is a reflection of a desire to maintain or improve their social position.

parents are willing to invest heavily in the provision of physical activity opportunities for young children, influenced by their social background, and that these investments can be perceived as attempts to maintain or improve their social position.

(1) parents perceive themselves as having a ‘responsibility' to aid their childrens' physical development, (2) parents are willing to provide their children with opportunities to develop physical capital, (3) parents from higher social class backgrounds are more likely to perceive the need to invest in physical capital and (4) parents are influenced by their own personal experiences, tastes and value when making decisions about physical capital.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which ‘middle-class’ families are investing in their children's futures, and the ways in which they are attempting to secure their children's social position through the acquisition of capital.
the role of the family and the home in facilitating the accumulation of capital and the development of habitus.
the role that early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings play in the reproduction of class-based habitus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the provision of preschool opportunities for physical development and physical activity can be viewed as a means by which parents can attempt to ensure the success of their children, and, in turn, themselves.
intensive mothering is a manifestation of the middle-class habitus and a mechanism for the reproduction of a social class position.
‘intensive’ mothering can be perceived as a form of ‘cultural reproduction’ (Bourdieu 1977) which, in this case, can be seen to contribute to the reproduction of a middle-class habitus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
‘middle-class parents’ are more likely than ‘working-class parents’ to provide physical activity and enrichment opportunities for their children in the early years.
parents are increasingly aware of the importance and impact that early years' provision can have on their child’s development.
parents of preschool children are aware of the need to equip their child with physical capital, which is seen to be a form of cultural capital.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for more in-depth research to explore the impact that the ‘intensive mother’ has on children's physical activity levels, particularly within the preschool years.

the ‘middle class’ is more likely to invest in the physical development of their child through the provision of enrichment opportunities and that this may be a means of reproducing class-based habitus, which may in turn have implications for physical development.

parents, particularly those from middle-class backgrounds, perceive a responsibility to provide copious enrichment activities for their children, with the aim of cultivating their physical capital and, ultimately, improving their social status and position.
